title: How to Thaw a Turkey for Thanksgiving 2026 (Safely and on Time)
seoTitle: How to Thaw a Turkey Safely for Thanksgiving 2026
excerpt: Frozen turkey thawing times by weight, the only three methods food safety agencies say are safe, and a countdown plan so your bird is ready by Thanksgiving 2026.
content:
Quick answer: Thaw a frozen turkey in the refrigerator, never on the counter. Allow about 24 hours for every 4 to 5 pounds (roughly 2 kg) of bird. A 12 to 14 pound turkey therefore needs about three full days in the fridge. The other two safe methods are a cold water bath, where the water is changed every 30 minutes and the turkey is cooked as soon as it is thawed, and the microwave, again cooked straight away. Your turkey must reach 165 degrees F (74 degrees C) all the way through in the oven.

Thanksgiving 2026 falls on Thursday, 26 November. If you buy a frozen bird, the clock starts the moment you put it in the fridge, and a big turkey runs out of time faster than most people expect. This guide uses the thawing rules published by the US Department of Agriculture and the UK Food Standards Agency, and turns them into a simple countdown you can follow at home.

How long does it take to thaw a turkey?

The refrigerator is the safest place to thaw any frozen meat, because it keeps the bird in the cold zone the whole time and bacteria cannot grow quickly. The US Department of Agriculture allows roughly 24 hours for every 4 to 5 pounds of weight. That figure is for a refrigerator set at 40 degrees F (4 degrees C) or below.

Turkey weightFridge thawing time (about)Start in the fridge
8 to 12 lb (3.5 to 5.5 kg)2 to 3 daysMonday 23 Nov or earlier
12 to 16 lb (5.5 to 7 kg)3 to 4 daysSunday 22 Nov or earlier
16 to 20 lb (7 to 9 kg)4 to 5 daysSaturday 21 Nov or earlier
20 to 24 lb (9 to 11 kg)5 to 6 daysFriday 20 Nov or earlier

These are guides, not guarantees. The UK Food Standards Agency gives a matching rule in metric: about 10 to 12 hours per kilogram in the fridge, and notes that a typical large 6 to 7 kg turkey can take as much as four days to thaw all the way to the middle. If your packaging carries its own thawing instructions, follow those first, since a commercial bird may be built slightly differently from a plain frozen one.

The safest approach is to plan for the longer end of the range. A turkey that has thawed a day early keeps perfectly well in the fridge, but a turkey that is still icy in the centre on Thanksgiving morning is a problem you cannot fix quickly without breaking the rules.

Can you thaw a turkey on the counter overnight?

No. Both the USDA and the Food Standards Agency are clear that a turkey should never be left to thaw at room temperature. In the temperature range between about 40 and 140 degrees F (4 to 60 degrees C), bacteria such as Salmonella multiply quickly, and the outside of a large bird can spend many hours in that danger zone while the inside is still frozen. The USDA lists the fridge, cold water and the microwave as the only safe ways to defrost food.

The counter-top shortcut is the most common turkey mistake, and it is also the one most likely to make people ill, because a big bird can look firm on the outside while its cavity is still warm and wet.

What are the three safe ways to thaw a turkey?

All three methods below come from official food safety guidance. Only the refrigerator method lets you refreeze the turkey or leave it for later. The other two require you to cook the bird straight away.

1. In the refrigerator (the best method)

Keep the turkey in its original wrapper, or set it in a tray or container with a rim to catch drips, and place it on the bottom shelf. The UK Food Standards Agency recommends a lidded container big enough to catch any liquid, so raw juices cannot drip onto other food. Wash your hands with soap and warm water after touching the bird, and clean any surface it has touched.

A 5 C (41 F) fridge is the target; check it with a cheap fridge thermometer rather than trusting the dial. Do not crowd the fridge, since cold air needs to move around the bird for even thawing. Once a fridge-thawed turkey is fully defrosted, it can stay in the fridge for a day or two before cooking, and it can be refrozen if you change your plan.

2. In cold water (faster, but cook it right away)

The cold water method is quicker, and it is the usual rescue when the fridge plan started late. Put the turkey in a leak-proof plastic bag, squeeze out the air, and submerge it in cold tap water. Change the water every 30 minutes so it stays cold, and allow about 30 minutes per pound. A 14 pound bird therefore takes around seven hours this way.

The water bath does not stay cold for long, which is why the change-every-half-hour rule matters. The USDA says food thawed in cold water must be cooked immediately, so this method rules out refreezing. If the bag leaks and water gets into the wrapper, treat the turkey as you would any raw poultry and cook it promptly.

3. In the microwave (only if it fits, and cook it now)

A microwave works only for a small turkey or a crown that fits on the turntable with room to rotate. Use the defrost setting and turn and rotate the bird as your microwave manual advises. Microwave thawing can start cooking the edges, so the USDA again says cook the turkey immediately afterwards and never refreeze it.

For most Thanksgiving-sized birds the microwave is impractical, so treat it as a backup for a small crown or a last-minute shop, not as the main plan.

How do you know the turkey is fully thawed?

Check the deepest, coldest parts: the centre of the breast, the thickest part of the thigh, and the cavity. Press the breast with a finger and feel for ice; open the legs slightly and feel inside the cavity with a clean hand or a probe. The juices should run clear and the meat should feel soft and give under pressure. If there is any ice or a hard spot, it needs more time.

A partly frozen turkey will not cook evenly. The outside can reach a safe temperature while the centre is still cold, which means harmful bacteria can survive. The UK Food Standards Agency warns in exactly these terms; a turkey that is not fully defrosted before cooking may cook unevenly, and that puts your guests at risk.

What should you do on Thanksgiving Day?

Take the thawed turkey out of the fridge only when you are ready to prepare it, and do not wash it. The Food Standards Agency advises against washing raw turkey, because splashing water spreads germs across your hands, clothes, worktops and utensils. Pat it dry with paper towels instead, and throw the towels away.

Cook the bird at the oven temperature the packaging recommends. If there are no instructions, the Food Standards Agency suggests a preheated oven at 180 C (350 F or Gas Mark 4): 45 minutes per kilogram plus 20 minutes for a bird under 4.5 kg, 40 minutes per kilogram for 4.5 to 6.5 kg, and 35 minutes per kilogram for anything over 6.5 kg. Cook stuffing in a separate tin, not inside the bird, because stuffing slows the cooking and can hide a cold spot.

The one number that matters is 165 F (74 C) in the thickest part of the meat, measured with a food thermometer. When you cut into the thickest part, the meat should not be pink and the juices should run clear.

What if you forgot to thaw the turkey in time?

Two options do not break the food safety rules. The first is the cold water method, which can thaw a mid-size bird in under a day. The second is to cook the turkey from frozen, but only if the packaging says it is safe; many whole frozen birds can be roasted from frozen, though they take roughly 50 percent longer and cook less evenly. Check the label before you try it, and never place a still-frozen bird on the counter to speed things up.

If neither works in the time you have, a fresh turkey or a smaller crown from the shop is a better answer than a half-thawed gamble.

How far ahead can you buy and store a frozen turkey?

A turkey sitting in the freezer at 0 F (-18 C) is safe almost indefinitely, because the freezer acts like a pause button for bacteria. Quality is another matter: most food safety bodies suggest eating frozen meat within a few months for the best texture, so buy in good time but do not hold a bird for a year.

You can also buy a fresh turkey a few days early and leave it in the fridge, following the use-by date on the label. Never partly thaw a bird, put it back in the freezer, then thaw it again at room temperature, as the repeated warm spells are exactly what bacteria need.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a 14 pound turkey take to thaw in the fridge?

About three to four days at 40 F (4 C) or below, following the USDA rule of 24 hours per 4 to 5 pounds. Start it by Sunday 22 November for Thanksgiving on Thursday 26 November.

Can you thaw a turkey at room temperature?

No. The USDA and the Food Standards Agency both say never thaw a turkey on the counter. Use the fridge, cold water or the microwave instead.

Can you refreeze a thawed turkey?

Only one thawed in the refrigerator can be safely refrozen. A turkey thawed in cold water or the microwave must be cooked immediately and cannot be refrozen.

Do you have to thaw a turkey before cooking it?

Most frozen turkeys need thawing. Some are sold ready to cook from frozen if the label says so, but they cook less evenly and take much longer, so check the packaging first.

How long can a thawed turkey stay in the fridge before cooking?

A fridge-thawed turkey can be kept for one to two days before cooking, as long as it stays at 40 F (4 C) or below and within its use-by date.

What temperature does the turkey need to reach?

165 F (74 C) in the thickest part of the meat, measured with a food thermometer. Check the thigh and the breast, since the thigh often takes longest.

This article covers food safety guidance from public health authorities. It is general information, not a substitute for the instructions on your turkey's packaging.
